name: Panama
summary: Separated from Colombia in 1903 with US support; the Panama Canal (1914) was handed to Panama in 1999.

location.value: The isthmus joining North and South America; about 75,000 km².

terrain.value: Mountains run along the centre, rising to Volcán Barú (about 3,475 m); lowlands on both coasts and the Darién rainforest in the east.

climate.value: Tropical, hot and humid, with a rainy season from about May to December and a drier season early in the year.

resources.value: Its position for the canal, Pacific and Caribbean fisheries, tropical forests, bananas, and copper deposits.

disasters.value: Floods and landslides in the rainy season; droughts, as in 2023, lower the lakes that feed the canal.

population.value: About 4 million people; the 2023 census counted about 4.06 million.

urbanisation.value: Mostly urban; Panama City holds about half the population, with other cities such as Colón and David.

disease.value: Yellow fever and malaria during canal building.

migration.value: Tens of thousands of workers from the Caribbean, especially Barbados and Jamaica, came to build the canal (1904–14).

economicBase.value: Canal tolls, banking, shipping and logistics, the Colón Free Zone, and tourism.

tradeRoutes.value: The Panama Canal (opened 1914, expanded locks 2016) carries a large share of world shipping between the Atlantic and Pacific.

wealth.value: A high-income economy and one of the richest in Latin America, though wealth is very unequally shared.

moneyAndTax.value: The balboa, fixed at par with the US dollar since 1904; in practice US dollar notes are used for paper money.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic: a president elected for five years and a single-chamber National Assembly.

keyRulers.value: Omar Torrijos (military ruler 1968–81, who signed the 1977 canal treaties) and Manuel Noriega (military ruler 1983–89).

succession.value: Free elections every five years since 1994, with power passing peacefully between parties; presidents cannot serve back-to-back terms.

institutions.value: The National Assembly, the Supreme Court, the Electoral Tribunal and the Panama Canal Authority, which runs the canal.

stability.value: Military rule from the 1968 coup until a US invasion removed Noriega in December 1989; democratic since then.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Abolished its army in 1990 and confirmed this in the constitution in 1994; it keeps police, border and air–naval services.

majorWars.value: The US invasion of December 1989 (Operation Just Cause), which removed Manuel Noriega from power.

territoryChange.value: The US-run Canal Zone was handed back in stages, ending with full control of the canal on 31 December 1999.

alliancesRivals.value: Closely tied to the United States since 1903; a member of the Organization of American States and the UN.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Panama (1935) and the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, famous for rainforest research.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The Panama Canal, the trans-isthmus railway, Tocumen airport as a regional hub, and the Panama City Metro (2014).

religion.value: Mostly Catholic, with a growing Protestant and evangelical minority and smaller Muslim, Jewish and other groups.

languageWriting.value: Spanish is the official language; Indigenous languages such as Ngäbere and Guna and Caribbean English are also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Colourful molas sewn by Guna women, the pollera dress, and the colonial Casco Viejo of Panama City.

sharedIdentity.value: National pride in the canal and in sovereignty over it, remembered in the protests of January 1964.

dailyLife.value: City life in apartments for many; foods include sancocho chicken stew, rice and beans, and plantains.

neighbours.value: Costa Rica to the west and Colombia to the east, across the roadless Darién Gap.

ideasReligions.value: Nationalist demands for control of the canal, which drove the 1964 protests and the 1977 Torrijos–Carter Treaties.

colonisation.value: Spanish from the 1500s, then part of Gran Colombia and Colombia from 1821 until separation in 1903.

riseSignals.value: Separated from Colombia on 3 November 1903 with US backing, then granted the US the Canal Zone.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; full control of the canal from 1999 brought strong economic growth.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic that owns and runs the Panama Canal.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
